origin_region: Amazon basin · Napo and Pastaza provinces (also Peru and Colombia)
cultivar: Ilex guayusa (a holly related to yerba mate)
processing: Leaves are hand-picked from trees grown in forest gardens (chakras), withered briefly, then dried with warm air or in the sun; some producers lightly toast the leaf. Sold as cut leaf, whole dried leaves, or in tea bags.
harvest_season: Year-round in the Amazon; mature leaves are picked from the same trees every few months, so there is no single harvest season.
appearance_dry: Large, leathery dark-olive leaves or coarse chopped pieces, tougher and glossier than tea leaf.
appearance_wet: Thick, rubbery whole leaves that barely soften, smelling of hay and green beans.
taste_profile: Smooth and mildly sweet, with hay, green beans and a soft earthy base; much less bitter than yerba mate and with almost no astringency, so long steeps stay drinkable.

brewing.notes: Just-off-the-boil water, 5–7 minutes; it does not turn bitter, so a second long steep or a 15-minute pot simmer (the traditional way, in a large pot before dawn) both work. Cold brew is clean and sweet.

vintage_note: Sold year-round with no harvest date, since the trees are picked continuously; packs carry a best-before of around two years and usually state organic or fair-trade certification and whether the leaf is whole, cut or bagged. Export guayusa only appeared in quantity in the 2010s, so most of what you see is from a handful of Ecuadorian cooperatives and brands. Freshly dried leaf is greener and sweeter; a brown, dusty cut is old stock.
description:
Guayusa is the caffeinated holly of the Ecuadorian Amazon, a cousin of yerba mate that the Kichwa people have long brewed in big pots before dawn and drunk together while planning the day. Outside Ecuador it was almost unknown until the 2010s, when it started appearing as loose leaf, tea bags and canned energy drinks.

The leaves are picked from trees grown in mixed forest gardens rather than plantations, then simply dried; there is no oxidation or long resting stage as with mate. That is why guayusa tastes so different from its relative: no smoke, little bitterness, just a smooth hay-sweet cup with a noticeable caffeine lift. The leaf is thick and leathery, so it gives up its flavour slowly and never turns harsh.

Brew it like a forgiving black tea, hot water and five to seven minutes, and expect something between a mild green tea and a sweet herbal infusion, with an earthy base. The traditional preparation is a long boil in a pot, which produces a darker, stronger drink; a cold brew gives a clean iced tea that needs no sugar. The main thing people get wrong is under-brewing it because they fear bitterness that never comes.

There is nothing to know about vintages: trees are picked all year and the leaf is sold with a simple best-before. Look for cut or whole leaf that is still olive-green rather than brown, and for the producer or cooperative named on the pack.

It is the easiest entry to the caffeinated South American hollies: try it before yerba mate if bitterness puts you off, or after mate if you want the same lift with a gentler cup.
